title: CREATE TABLE and Data Types
summary: CREATE TABLE makes a new table and names its columns. Each column stores one kind of fact.
introduction: CREATE TABLE makes a new table and names its columns. Each column stores one kind of fact. Design a small book list. Choose columns for a title and page count, then decide which facts every row must have.
learningObjectives: Create a table with typed columns, NOT NULL and DEFAULT
Choose data types that work across SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL
Explain how auto-generated ids differ between databases
Modify and remove tables with ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE

blocks.text: A `CREATE TABLE` statement lists the columns, each with a type and optional rules. `NOT NULL` requires a value, `DEFAULT` supplies one when the insert omits the column, and `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` makes `id` the unique, auto-numbered identifier of each row.

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE employees (
OK: INSERT INTO employees (name, department, salary, hired_on)
OK: INSERT INTO employees (name, department, salary, hired_on, remote)

id | name        | department  | salary | hired_on   | remote
---+-------------+-------------+--------+------------+-------
1  | Nia Patel   | Engineering | 72000  | 2025-03-01 | 0
2  | Omar Haddad | Design      | 58000  | 2025-04-15 | 1

blocks.text: The first insert omits `remote`, so it receives the default 0; the second sets it explicitly.
The SQL standard defines types such as `INTEGER`, `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `DATE` and `BOOLEAN`, but every database implements its own set. These choices transfer well:

SQLite is special: it uses *type affinity*. A column's declared type is a preference, not a rule, so you can store text in an `INTEGER` column unless the table is declared `STRICT` (SQLite 3.37+). `VARCHAR(50)` is accepted but the length is not enforced. `TRUE` and `FALSE` are just aliases for 1 and 0, and dates are text, which is why the ISO format matters so much. The `typeof()` function reveals what was actually stored:

blocks.code:
SELECT typeof(42) AS integer_value,
       typeof(4.2) AS real_value,
       typeof('42') AS text_value,
       typeof(NULL) AS null_value,
       typeof(TRUE) AS boolean_value;

blocks.content:
integer_value | real_value | text_value | null_value | boolean_value
--------------+------------+------------+------------+--------------
integer       | real       | text       | null       | integer

blocks.title: Floating point is wrong for money
blocks.text: `REAL`, `FLOAT` and `DOUBLE` cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums of prices drift: `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. Use `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` with a fixed scale in PostgreSQL and MySQL, and in SQLite store integer cents (`2475` for 24.75) or round at output with `ROUND()`. The sample `products.price` column uses `REAL` for simplicity, which is why the lessons round their totals.

Every database can number rows for you, but the syntax differs. SQLite: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` is an alias for the internal row id and auto-numbers; adding `AUTOINCREMENT` guarantees that the numbers of deleted rows are never reused. PostgreSQL: `id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` (or the older `SERIAL`). MySQL: `id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY`. SQL Server: `id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY`.

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE notes (
OK: INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES ('Buy milk'), ('Call Ada')
OK: DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = 2
OK: INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES ('Ship v2')

id | body     | status
---+----------+-------
1  | Buy milk | draft
3  | Ship v2  | draft

blocks.text: After deleting note 2, the next insert received id 3 because of `AUTOINCREMENT`; without it SQLite would have reused 2 (it assigns the largest existing id plus one). Reusing ids is rarely what you want when other systems remember them.

Tables evolve. `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` adds a column (existing rows get the default or NULL); `RENAME COLUMN` and `DROP COLUMN` rename or remove one (SQLite supports them since 3.25 and 3.35). `DROP TABLE` deletes the table and all its rows; `IF EXISTS` avoids an error when it is already gone.

blocks.content:
OK: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN stock INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
OK: UPDATE products SET stock = 25 WHERE id = 1

id | name      | stock
---+-----------+------
1  | Notebook  | 25
2  | Mouse pad | 0

blocks.text: In SQLite the `sqlite_master` table lists every table, index and view in the database, the equivalent of MySQL's `SHOW TABLES` or the `\dt` command in psql. After creating and dropping a temporary table, only the three sample tables remain:

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE temp_list (value TEXT)
OK: DROP TABLE temp_list

name
---------
customers
products
orders

questions.question: Which type should hold a price such as 24.75 in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: NUMERIC (or DECIMAL) with a fixed scale stores decimals exactly. REAL is binary floating point and drifts, TEXT cannot be summed, and INTEGER would only work for cents.

questions.question: In SQLite, `TRUE` is stored as the integer 1.
questions.explanation: SQLite has no boolean type; TRUE and FALSE are keywords for the integers 1 and 0, as typeof(TRUE) shows.
